name: chem-deep-mc-plan-r1
context:
A PLAN FOR A SECOND MONTE CARLO RUN, ON THE TWO MECHANICS THE FIRST RUN'S FINDINGS POINT AT. Submitted before any code is written. Nothing here is built.

─────────── WHY THESE TWO AND NOT THE OTHER FORTY-EIGHT ───────────

The first run closed with your verdict that this design "cannot be a Deep Strategy game; it is a game of maximizing efficiency within a set of visible constraints". Fifty candidate mechanics were drafted against that. Two survive the run's own findings, and the other forty-eight are ruled out by one measurement or another:

  · INFORMATION IS RULED OUT. Preview bought 31.6 points of agency floor by
    spending 47 points of solver margin; the planner went from 63% to 88% of the
    ceiling. Showing the player more converts unreachable ceiling into reachable
    skill. It does not create skill.

  · CHEAP STRUCTURAL CHANGES ARE RULED OUT, and I know because I tested my own
    top-ranked idea before building it. A new metric, CONSEQUENCE HORIZON: fork
    at turn 0, one branch takes the readable rule's best move and the other a
    different legal move, then BOTH play identically on the identical seed. Any
    final gap belongs to that one move.

        refill POOL (all prior work)   one move worth 0.38 of a 4.94 score
        refill VOID (no refill)        one move worth 0.30 of a 2.64 score
        VOID + positional delivery     one move worth 0.00 of a 1.23 score

    EVERY GAP IS BELOW 1. A single move is worth less than one delivery. The game
    is not merely shallow, it is SELF-CORRECTING: a worse opening move costs
    almost nothing because the readable rule recovers from it. No-refill raises
    the relative share only by halving the score, and adding a dock makes the
    opening move literally irrelevant.

So depth has to come from something a greedy policy CANNOT RECOVER FROM. That is one property, and exactly two of the fifty have it.

─────────── MECHANIC ONE: THE DECLARED ROUTE (commitment) ───────────

Before executing, the player DECLARES a target from the open book and commits to delivering it within N turns. Completion pays a multiple; failure forfeits a stake from the bank.

Why a greedy policy cannot recover: the stake is sunk at declaration. A player who declares the wrong target has already paid, and no subsequent optimal play refunds it. This is the first decision in the game whose cost is not recoverable by playing well afterwards, which is precisely what the consequence-horizon measurement says is missing.

It is also the first mechanic here that makes the player's own uncertainty the subject. Declaring is a bet on your own read of the board.

─────────── MECHANIC TWO: THE SHARED BOARD (opponent) ───────────

Two players alternate on ONE board with SEPARATE books. The resource in contention is the board itself. Your earlier ruling on the co-op design applies and is why this shape rather than a shared pot: "it moves the conflict from 'I am stealing your points' to 'I am taking the path you needed'... a common enemy in the dwindling connectivity of the board."

Why a greedy policy cannot recover: an opponent is not a distribution. A beam search can solve a board; it cannot solve a person, and it cannot recover from an opponent having taken the atoms it needed. DENIAL -- consuming what the other player's book requires -- is the first genuinely strategic negative action in the design.

─────────── THE METHODOLOGICAL PROBLEM I AM RAISING BEFORE YOU FIND IT ───────────

EVERY GATE THIS PROJECT USES ASSUMES A SOLITAIRE CEILING, AND VERSUS HAS NONE.

AGENCY FLOOR is planner-over-readable-rule. SOLVER MARGIN is ceiling-over-planner. Both presume a well-defined best play on a fixed board. In a two-player game the best play is a function of the opponent, there is no single ceiling, and a beam search against a fixed opponent measures that opponent rather than the game.

So versus needs a different instrument, and I propose:

    HEAD-TO-HEAD LADDER   does a deeper agent beat a shallower one, over paired
                          seeds with sides swapped so the deal cannot favour a
                          side? Report win rate, not score.
    EXPLOITABILITY        how much does a best-response agent, allowed to see
                          the opponent's policy, gain over the policy it faces?
                          Low exploitability across a ladder means the strategy
                          space is rich rather than solved.
    DENIAL VALUE          a denial-aware agent against an identical agent with
                          denial disabled. If it is zero, the shared board is a
                          shared table and not a shared resource.

I would rather be told this instrument is wrong now than discover it in the results, which is what happened to three evaluators in the first run.

─────────── THE STAGES, UNCHANGED ───────────

STAGE 0 - INSTRUMENT VALIDATION, with the first run's controls plus four new ones:
    N1 the declared route's stake is actually forfeit on failure (negative control:
       a version that refunds it must score strictly higher);
    N2 a declaration cannot be retroactively changed -- the executor rejects a
       second declaration for the same slot;
    N3 in versus, swapping sides on the same seed swaps the result, so the
       instrument carries no side bias;
    N4 a self-play agent against itself wins 50% +/- sampling error. If it does
       not, the side-swap is broken and every versus number is worthless.

STAGE 1 - SCREENING, resolution V or better, recomputed from the sign matrix rather than asserted. Factors: ROUTE on/off, route STAKE size, route WINDOW length, DENIAL on/off, OPPONENT DEPTH, and OPTIONS carried forward as the one validated mechanic.

STAGE 2 - full factorial on survivors. STAGE 3 - confirmation on disjoint seeds. STAGE 4 - exploit sweep, with two new attacks specific to these mechanics: declaring a target already sitting on the board (a free stake), and stalling in versus so the opponent exhausts the board first. STAGE 5 - population and the dual constraint.

─────────── PRE-REGISTERED ACCEPTANCE ───────────

    CONSEQUENCE HORIZON   >= 1.0   one move worth at least one delivery. This is
                                   the new primary response and the bar is the
                                   weakest defensible one: a move should be worth
                                   at least what it immediately pays.
    AGENCY FLOOR          >= 25%   solitaire modes only
    SOLVER MARGIN         > 0      instrument sanity
    HEAD-TO-HEAD          >= 60%   a deeper agent beats a shallower one
    DENIAL VALUE          > 0      the shared board is a contested resource
    DOMINATED             false
    THROUGHPUT            2.0-8.0

SEED SHARE is NOT a gate in this run and the reason is recorded rather than quietly dropped: the first run established a null floor of 19.5% manufactured by scoring small integers, so the 35% bar was measuring two things at once. Re-specifying it is a human decision that has not been made, so it is reported and not gated.

─────────── WHAT WOULD MAKE ME ABANDON ───────────

  · consequence horizon stays below 1.0 under every combination, which would mean
    the self-correction is a property of the chemistry rather than of the verbs,
    and no mechanic fixes it;
  · the declared route's best strategy is "never declare", making it a dead
    button;
  · denial value is zero, meaning the shared board is cosmetic;
  · head-to-head is near 50% across a depth ladder, meaning depth does not win.

questions.text: Every gate this project uses assumes a solitaire ceiling and versus has none. I propose a head-to-head ladder, exploitability, and denial value instead. Is that the right instrument, and what does it miss that agency floor and solver margin were catching?

CONSEQUENCE HORIZON becomes the primary response, with a bar of 1.0 — one move worth at least one delivery. Is that bar defensible, or is it arbitrary in the same way the imported 35% seed-share bar turned out to be?

The declared route's claim is that a sunk stake cannot be recovered by later optimal play. What is the strongest argument that a good player simply never declares unless it is already safe, making the mechanic a formality rather than a commitment?

I ruled out 48 of 50 mechanics on two measurements — the preview/solver-margin trade and the consequence-horizon test of no-refill. Is that a legitimate narrowing, or am I generalising from two data points to a whole design space?
Name the failure mode that neither the stages, the new controls N1-N4, nor the pre-registered acceptance would catch in THIS run.
